extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency counsel, litigators, and judges interested in notice-and-comment remedial doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal criteria and evaluative standards courts use to judge the adequacy of notice-and-comment procedures and to choose remedies (vacatur, remand, harmless-error treatment) for APA procedural violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical-outgrowth / Reasonably specific notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule; the public must have been given "reasonably specific notice" that the alternative adopted in the final rule was among the range of alternatives being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the final rule adopts a change (e.g., bright-line distance limitations) that was not reasonably specific in the proposal (e.g., a standard-based proposal), courts may find a logical-outgrowth violation and vacate the rule. Example: Sixth Circuit held states had a substantial chance of prevailing because the proposal used a standard while the final rule adopted bright-line distances and the public lacked reasonably specific notice. Agencies should articulate particular alternatives (specific limits/distances) in the proposal if they intend to adopt them in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of notice required (standards versus bright-line shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of specificity required in a proposal—especially when shifting from an open-ended standard to bright-line rules—matters; vague or open-ended proposals can create a logical-outgrowth problem if the final rule is more specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies that propose an open-ended 'best professional judgments' standard but later adopt specific geographic limits or distance cutoffs risk procedural invalidation unless the proposal gave adequate notice of those specific alternatives. The agencies' failure to 'spell out the particular limits and distances' can be fatal even if the topic was broadly discussed in the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to show what commenters would have said (prejudice/focus requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts sometimes require challengers to show that they would have submitted additional or different comments and that those comments could have altered the agency's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some decisions demand a showing that inadequate notice caused prejudice by preventing focused opposition; other courts (and commentators) criticize this requirement as unduly onerous, especially where the record already contains specific comments addressing the issue. Examples: the Sixth Circuit did not require states to explain what they would have said; the Allina decision faulted the challengers even though detailed comments existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error skepticism in notice-and-comment cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are generally skeptical of applying the harmless-error doctrine to agency failures to observe notice-and-comment procedures; many circuits and courts favor vacatur over treating the omission as harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D.C. Circuit and others have stated they are 'not hospitable to government claims of harmless error' in §553 failures; commentators (Hickman & Thomson) argue for a strong presumption that postpublication comment can't cure notice-and-comment errors. Nonetheless, in some instances (and circuits) courts have accepted a harmless-error approach where the record shows the agency would not have acted differently or the affected parties had ample opportunity to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency engagement and breadth of outreach as evidence against prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive engagement with stakeholders—meetings, advisory boards, scientific reports, thousands of comments—can demonstrate that the regulated community had meaningful notice and opportunity to comment and therefore may undercut claims of prejudice from imperfect notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records showing broad outreach (e.g., hundreds of meetings, SAB review, long comment docket, targeted meetings with affected parties) are evidence that regulated parties had ample opportunity to influence the outcome. Courts should consider these indicia when assessing whether procedural defects actually harmed interested parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpublication/postpromulgation notice-and-comment as a possible cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether inviting comments after promulgation cures an initial notice defect depends on whether the agency kept an open mind and made a 'compelling showing' that it remained receptive to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The D.C. Circuit allows postpublication comment to cure defects if the agency demonstrates it kept an open mind; other circuits (e.g., Fifth Circuit) resist this cure, fearing agencies could evade pre-promulgation comment by republishing later. Courts examine whether the postpromulgation process was genuine (agency responsiveness, willingness to change). Scholarly views diverge—some urge a strong presumption against curing by postpublication comment, others see greater flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception: narrow construction and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may invoke the APA's good-cause exception to dispense with notice-and-comment when notice is 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest,' but courts construe that exception narrowly and review such determinations closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts sometimes give no particular deference to agency good-cause findings (e.g., D.C. Circuit); circuits are divided on whether review is de novo or arbitrary/abuse-of-discretion. Vacatur is the conventional remedy if a court finds that good cause was improperly invoked. Example: SORNA interim final rule generated split circuit treatment—some circuits upheld good cause for urgent public safety reasons; others vacated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration versus technical correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a post-issuance change or an amendment is a mere technical correction or instead materially alters regulated parties' obligations determines whether notice-and-comment is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency's change increases regulatory obligations or changes who is regulated (material alteration), it cannot be tacked on as a mere technical correction without notice-and-comment. Example: EPA's 'surface concentration' wording for porous materials—alleged to be a clerical mistake—was held to materially alter obligations and the court vacated the change despite the agency's claim it was a correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of agency responses to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts evaluate whether agencies have adequately responded to submitted comments; a 'palpably inadequate' response can be the basis for invalidating a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when agency followed notice-and-comment, a deficient response in the final rule's preamble or explanation (e.g., disregarding central objections or failing to explain why comments were rejected) can lead to remand or vacatur. Example: the D.C. Circuit vacated CAB's reissued rule because the agency's response to comments was palpably inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial choice: vacatur as default but subject to contextual critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacatur is the conventional judicial remedy for procedural APA violations, but commentators argue that courts sometimes apply 'remedial purity' too rigidly—even where procedural error likely produced no prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts typically vacate rules adopted without notice-and-comment or with logical-outgrowth failures; however, the article criticizes this practice where the agency engaged stakeholders and the record shows parties had meaningful opportunities to comment. Some circuits have declined to vacate in narrow circumstances (e.g., Fifth Circuit in SORNA). Courts should weigh the functions of notice-and-comment (informed decisionmaking, legitimacy, participation) against the costs of vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of criminal consequences in harmless-error analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a procedurally defective rule produces criminal liability or convictions, courts are especially reluctant to deem the procedural error harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential for criminal sanctions or convictions (as in SORNA's retroactivity determinations) makes courts less willing to accept post-hoc cures or harmless-error reasoning; courts emphasize the need for careful prior deliberation when individual liberty is at stake.
